v-jugularis-externa.summary: Vein collecting the superficial blood of the scalp and face, visible under the skin on the side of the neck.
facts: Behind the angle of the mandible, by the union of the posterior branch of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein
Descends obliquely across the sternocleidomastoid
Subclavian vein
clinical: It becomes prominent when right heart pressure rises; in emergencies it can be used for venous access.
tus: The EJV is formed by the union of the posterior branch of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein.

v-subclavia.summary: Continuation of the axillary vein, collecting blood from the deep and superficial veins of the arm.
facts: Continuation of the axillary vein at the outer border of the 1st rib
Passes in front of the anterior scalene (unlike the artery) and behind the clavicle
Joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein
External jugular vein
clinical: It is used for infraclavicular central venous catheterisation; pneumothorax is an important complication of the procedure.
Paget–Schroetter syndrome: subclavian vein thrombosis after strenuous arm exercise.
tus: Paget–Schroetter syndrome is effort thrombosis of the subclavian vein due to repetitive use of the arm.

vv-membri-superioris.tr: Superficial veins of the upper limb
vv-membri-superioris.summary: Superficial veins that begin in the dorsal venous network of the hand and rise under the skin of the arm: the cephalic vein (lateral), the basilic vein (medial) and the median cubital vein linking them at the elbow.
facts: Begins on the lateral side of the dorsum of the hand, rises on the lateral side of the arm and passes through the deltopectoral groove to drain into the axillary vein
Begins on the medial side of the dorsum of the hand, goes deep at mid-arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein
Runs obliquely from the cephalic to the basilic vein in the cubital fossa
Paired veins accompanying the arteries (venae comitantes): radial, ulnar and brachial veins
clinical: The median cubital vein is used most often for blood sampling and cannulation; beneath it, protected by the bicipital aponeurosis, lie the brachial artery and the median nerve.
The cephalic vein can be used to place pacemaker leads.
tus: The deep veins of the upper limb are paired veins accompanying the arteries (venae comitantes).

v-portae-hepatis.summary: Vein carrying nutrient-rich blood from the digestive tract, spleen, pancreas and gallbladder to the liver. It provides about 75% of the blood reaching the liver.
facts: Behind the neck of the pancreas, by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins (the inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the splenic vein)
Runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament, behind the bile duct (anterior right) and the proper hepatic artery (anterior left), to the porta hepatis
Right and left branches; ends in the hepatic sinusoids

Lower oesophagus (gastric veins – azygos vein), rectum (superior rectal – middle/inferior rectal veins), around the umbilicus (paraumbilical veins – veins of the abdominal wall), retroperitoneal veins
clinical: When portal hypertension develops, for example in cirrhosis, the anastomoses form oesophageal varices (fatal bleeding), haemorrhoids and dilated veins around the umbilicus (caput medusae); the spleen enlarges and ascites develops.
tus: The portal vein provides ~75% of the blood and ~50% of the oxygen reaching the liver.
Portal vein thrombosis is the commonest cause of prehepatic portal hypertension.

v-azygos.summary: Vein that collects blood from the posterior walls of the chest and abdomen and rises on the right of the spine to drain into the superior vena cava. It forms an important collateral route between the venae cavae.
facts: Union of the right ascending lumbar and subcostal veins (L1–L2)
Enters the chest through the aortic hiatus, rises on the right of the vertebral bodies and arches over the root of the right lung at T4 to drain into the superior vena cava
Right posterior intercostal veins, hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins (from the left), oesophageal and bronchial veins
clinical: When the IVC is blocked, the azygos system is an important collateral route for blood from the lower body to return to the heart.
tus: The hemiazygos vein crosses in front of the spine to the right at T8–T9 and opens into the azygos vein.
The azygos lobe is an anatomical variant in which the azygos vein is embedded in the apex of the right lung.

v-femoralis.summary: Large deep vein that collects the deep venous blood of the leg and runs with the femoral artery.
facts: Continuation of the popliteal vein at the adductor hiatus
Rises behind the artery in the adductor canal and medial to it in the femoral triangle
Passes under the inguinal ligament to become the external iliac vein
Profunda femoris vein, great saphenous vein (saphenofemoral junction)
clinical: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) develops most often in the deep veins of the leg; if the clot breaks off and reaches the lung it causes pulmonary embolism.
In emergencies a catheter can be placed in the femoral vein just medial to the femoral pulse.
tus: In the groin the femoral vein lies medial to the artery; it can be used for central venous catheterisation.
Deep vein thrombosis is most common in the femoropopliteal segment.

v-saphena-magna.summary: The longest vein of the body; it rises under the skin on the inner side of the leg from the medial edge of the dorsum of the foot to the groin.
facts: Medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot
Passes in front of the medial malleolus (constant position), rises on the inner side of the leg with the saphenous nerve, behind the medial side of the knee and along the inner thigh
Passes through the saphenous opening to drain into the femoral vein in the groin (saphenofemoral junction)
Contains 10–20 valves; joined to the deep veins by perforating veins
clinical: Valve incompetence leads to varicose veins.
It is often used as a graft in coronary bypass surgery (reversed because of its valves).
Its constant position in front of the medial malleolus is used for emergency venous access (venous cut-down).
tus: The great saphenous vein is linked to the deep veins by perforating veins; valve incompetence causes varicose veins.
The superficial external pudendal, superficial epigastric and superficial circumflex iliac veins open at the saphenofemoral junction.

v-saphena-parva.summary: Superficial vein that begins at the lateral edge of the foot, rises on the back of the calf and drains into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
facts: Lateral end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot
Passes behind the lateral malleolus and rises in the middle of the calf with the sural nerve
Popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa
clinical: It can be the source of varicose veins on the back of the calf.
tus: The sural nerve can be injured in small saphenous vein surgery, causing numbness along the lateral edge of the foot.

sinus-durae-matris.summary: Valveless venous channels between the two layers of the dura mater that collect the venous blood of the brain and the CSF and pass them to the internal jugular vein.
facts: Superior and inferior sagittal sinuses, straight sinus, confluence of sinuses, transverse sinus, sigmoid sinus, occipital sinus, cavernous sinus, superior and inferior petrosal sinuses
Superior sagittal sinus → confluence of sinuses → transverse sinus → sigmoid sinus → internal jugular vein
The internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve pass through it; the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves run in its lateral wall
clinical: Infections in the 'danger triangle' of the face can spread through the ophthalmic vein to the cavernous sinus and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Dural venous sinus thrombosis presents with headache, seizures and raised intracranial pressure.
tus: The dural sinuses have no valves; through emissary veins they communicate with veins outside the skull.
Dural sinus thrombosis may present with headache, papilloedema and haemorrhagic infarction; pregnancy and oral contraceptives are risk factors.
